summary: Describes the Camellia encryption algorithm, a block cipher with a 128-bit block size and keys of 128, 192 or 256 bits. The document gives the algorithm, including its key schedule and data-mixing steps. It is informational, meant to let implementers work from a public description.

plainLanguage.summary: Camellia is a block cipher: it transforms a fixed-size block of data using a secret key. This memo describes how to create its subkeys, encrypt a block, and reverse the process to decrypt it.

subtitle: How the Camellia block cipher turns a fixed-size input into ciphertext using a secret key.

tldr.problem: Implementers need a precise description of Camellia, including how it prepares keys and transforms data.
tldr.mechanism: The cipher divides a 128-bit block into two halves and repeatedly combines them with subkeys in a Feistel structure. The key schedule derives those subkeys from a 128-, 192-, or 256-bit key.
tldr.outcome: The memo publishes the algorithm, CBC-mode object identifiers, and example input and output values. It is Informational and does not define an Internet standard.

today: RFC 3713 is Informational. The work-unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, and the memo says it does not specify an Internet standard.

sections.title: Camellia and Its Inputs
sections.content:
Camellia is a block cipher jointly developed by Nippon Telegraph and Telephone Corporation and Mitsubishi Electric Corporation. It processes a 128-bit block and accepts keys of 128, 192, or 256 bits. The memo describes the algorithm rather than defining an Internet protocol.

The design is divided into a key-scheduling part and a data-randomizing part. The first derives the values used during encryption; the second transforms the input block into ciphertext.
sections.plainLanguage: Camellia changes one 128-bit block at a time using a secret key. The key can have one of three lengths, and the memo explains both key preparation and data encryption.

sections.title: How the Key Schedule Works
sections.content:
The key schedule first represents the supplied key as two 128-bit values, KL and KR. A 128-bit key sets KR to zero; longer keys supply additional bits for KR, with the 192-bit form using the complement of its final 64 bits for the remaining portion.

The schedule combines these values with six fixed constants through the F-function to derive KA and, for longer keys, KB. It then rotates KL, KR, KA, and KB and selects 64-bit halves to form the whitening keys, round keys, and FL-function keys used by encryption.
sections.plainLanguage: The key schedule rearranges the secret key and combines it with fixed constants. It produces smaller subkeys that the encryption steps use in sequence.

sections.title: Encrypting and Decrypting a Block
sections.content:
Camellia splits a 128-bit plaintext block into two 64-bit halves. For a 128-bit key, encryption uses an 18-round Feistel structure; for 192- and 256-bit keys, it uses 24 rounds. Each round applies the F-function to one half and combines its result with the other half and a round subkey.

Before and after the rounds, the halves are combined with whitening keys. FL and its inverse are inserted after groups of six rounds. Decryption follows the same structure with the subkeys used in reverse order.
sections.plainLanguage: Encryption splits the block into two halves and repeatedly mixes one half into the other. Decryption uses the same operations with the subkeys in reverse order.

sections.title: The Functions Inside the Cipher
sections.content:
The F-function takes 64-bit input data and a 64-bit subkey. It combines them, divides the result into eight bytes, substitutes each byte using one of four lookup tables, and mixes the substituted bytes with XOR operations to produce 64 output bits.

The FL-function operates on two 32-bit halves using bitwise AND, OR, and XOR operations and a one-bit rotation. FLINV is its inverse. The memo defines the lookup tables and the exact operations needed to implement each function.
sections.plainLanguage: The F-function changes each byte through a lookup table and then mixes the bytes together. FL and FLINV are paired operations used between groups of rounds.

sections.title: CBC Identifiers and Test Data
sections.content:
The memo assigns separate object identifiers to Camellia with 128-, 192-, and 256-bit keys in Cipher Block Chaining mode. These uses require an initialization vector represented as an OCTET STRING of size 16. The plaintext is padded before encryption according to RFC 2315.

An appendix gives hexadecimal keys, plaintext blocks, and ciphertext blocks for each supported key length. These examples let an implementation compare its output with the values printed in the memo.
sections.plainLanguage: The memo gives identifiers for the three Camellia key lengths in CBC mode and specifies the required starting value. It also provides examples that can be used to check an implementation.
